newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - N.Korea food shortage to last years - US aides.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - N.Korea food shortage to last years - US aides.

text.p: North Korea is likely to remain short of food for many years to come, even if they have a favorable harvest this year, U.S. aides surveyed by Reuters said.

"I think, even under the best of circumstances, North Korea will remain a food-deficit country," said Lynn Rogers, acting assistant administrator of the US Agency for International Development's Bureau for Humanitarian Response.
That means despite North Korea's goal of self-reliance, it will need food aid or commercial imports "to feed its people" for the indefinite future, he said.
"The shortfall is bigger than agricultural improvement in North Korea alone can overcome," said John Dyck, an analsyt in the U.S. Agriculture Department's Economic Research Service.

North Korea's population is already too big for it to feed itself. "The key in my mind is they will have to be able to trade," Dyck said. Otherwise, they will remain dependent on the generosity of food donor nations such as the United States.
According to UN estimates, North Korea still faces a shortfall of 1 million tonnes of food this year.
While North Korean leaders attribute the severe shortfall to floods in 1995 and 1996, most of the blame rests with its state-run and highly inefficient agricultural system, the aides said.

One of its main crops beside rice is corn, which is ill-suited to North Korean's cold, northern climate. To get it to grow at all, it has be transplanted by hand from seed pots where individual plants have been started.

North Korea is the "only country in the world that does that," Dyck said. It's an extremely labor intensive process to produce a crop that can total 2 million tonnes, he said. The United States is now considering a U.N. World Food Program request for more food aid for North Korea. Over the past two years, the United States has already contributed $33.4 million, most of which has been corn.

While many Asian nations might turn their nose up at that grain, North Korea has converted corn into a rice lookalike for decades, Dyck said. That's a legacy of when it was part of the Japanese empire and had to ship all its rice to Japan.
Corn is also the cheapest grain on the world market. So in negotiations with donor nations, North Korea is inisting on corn "more and more," Dyck said.
What North Korea really needs to do is to reform its agriculture system, Rogers said, while emphasizing that the U.S. is not having any discussion with North Korea about helping them do that.

And while U.S. officials have some "broad ideas" about the problems facing North Korea's farm sector, "we really don't know as much as we should" because of the highly secretive nature of the Pyongyang regime, he said.

However, it appears clear that most of North Korea's difficulties stem from its "very-input intensive monoculture," Rogers said. For years, North Korea has planted the same crops on the same land and maintained yields by "pumping in the fertilizer," he said.

But with the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe and the Former Soviet Union, its trade sources for fertilizer and pesticides have dissappeared. As a result, yields have fallen sharply, Rogers said.

"It would require substantial change on their part" before the U.S. could even comtemplate providing technical or economic assistance to help boost North Korea," Rogers said. Currently, anti-terrorism and other laws prohibit such aid.

"I don't know what the future holds," Rogers said, when asked then if it was likely that the United States and other donors will be asked again and again over the next several years to provide food aid for North Korea.
It's difficult even to know how much the North Koreans "understand the nature of their problem," he said.
